1.goal: To open the lesson on a number she has had to explain at work, and to tell her what the lesson ends with.
run: Ask whether she did the pre-class and whether anything in it was unclear.
Tell her what the lesson ends with, in one sentence: an update on three numbers on a call, with questions about when they changed.
Ask the question on screen and take one answer.
exact: What today is: “Today you give an update on how three numbers have changed, and I ask you when they changed.”
If she names a number and stops: “What was it before, and what is it now?”
1.expected: One indicator and a sentence or two about it. A complete answer looks like “Absenteeism. It went up a lot after the pandemic, and I had to explain it every month.” Any number she brings is right here.
1.support: If nothing comes to mind, offer two: turnover or overtime.
1.challenge: Ask who she explained it to, and what they asked her.
1.monitoring: Whether a time word appears in her answer, and which verb comes with it.
1.evidence: The number she named, in her words.
1.transition: Move on when she has named one number.

2.goal: To hear, before any model, how she describes changes in numbers across different periods.
2.interaction: S–T, spoken, with the dashboard and the three questions on screen.
run: Read the question and the dashboard with her.
Let her describe the three numbers, using the three questions. Answer briefly if she asks you something.
Leave corrections for later in the lesson. Write down one sentence as she said it: it comes back on screen 6.
exact: If she only reads the figures: “And what has happened since the second quarter?”
2.expected: There is no answer key on this screen: it is the version she already has. A complete answer covers the three questions, for example “In the second quarter turnover went up from 9.2 to 14.6, and since then it has gone up a little more. Overtime went from 13 to 30 hours. Absenteeism has not changed.” Note which verb comes with a closed period (the second quarter) and which with an open one (since then).
2.support: If she cannot start, point at turnover and ask only the first question.
2.challenge: Ask which of the three numbers she would put first in an update, and why.
2.monitoring: Whether the present perfect appears for “since then”, and whether the second quarter gets the past simple.
2.evidence: One sentence she said, word for word. It is the sentence she looks at again on screen 6.
2.transition: Move on when she has described the three numbers.

3.goal: To read the same numbers in an email written by someone else, for meaning, before looking at form.
run: Give her about a minute and a half for the email.
Ask the question on screen.
Then ask which of Alison's sentences says something she did not say on screen 2.
3.expected: Turnover is the number still going up: “it has gone up again since July, to 15.1%.” Of the 40 people hired in May, “so far, 22 of them have stayed.” Absenteeism “has not moved much this year.”
3.support: If she answers with all the figures, ask for the one that is still moving.
3.challenge: Ask what Alison would probably want to discuss on Friday.
3.monitoring: Whether she notices the verbs in bold. Nothing needs to be said about them here.
3.evidence: Whether she found the number that is still going up without help.
3.transition: Move on when she has answered both parts of the question.

4.goal: To classify six sentences from the email by the kind of period they talk about.
4.interaction: S says each answer; T chooses it on screen. Then T–S.
run: For each of the six sentences, she says which period it is about and you choose it on screen. Then press Check.
Go through them out loud. On each, ask her which words tell her whether the period is over.
Leave the verb for the next screen: here she only looks at the period.
exact: On each sentence: “Which words tell you the period is over, or still open?”
4.expected: A period that is over: “Turnover rose from 9.2% to 14.6% in the second quarter.” · “We hired 40 people in May.” · “Overtime went from 13 to 30 hours a week between January and June.” A period that is still open: “It has gone up again since July.” · “So far, 22 of them have stayed.” · “Absenteeism has not moved much this year.” The time words that decide: in the second quarter, in May, between January and June; since July, so far, this year.
4.support: On each sentence, ask: could this number still change before the period ends?
4.challenge: Ask her to make one of the closed sentences open, and say what word she had to change.
4.monitoring: Whether she looks at the time words or guesses from the meaning.
4.evidence: Which sentence, if any, she placed in the wrong period.
4.transition: Move on when the six are classified.

5.goal: To have her connect the time words with the verb form, and state the pattern before the reveal.
run: Read the two pairs and the question with her.
Let her answer before you open the button. Accept the pattern in her own words.
Open the pattern and read it with her. Then ask her for one sentence of each kind about her own work.
exact: If she does not see it: “In the second quarter. Since July. Which of the two is over?”
Asking for her own sentences: “Tell me one thing that happened last year, and one thing that has happened this year.”
5.expected: Time words that close the period (in the second quarter, in May) go with rose and hired; time words that keep the period open until now (since July, so far) go with has gone up and have stayed. From the reveal: the past simple usually goes with a period that is over, and the present perfect usually goes with a period that is still open. Her own pair can be as simple as “Last year we hired twenty people. This year we have hired twelve so far.”
5.support: Cover the second pair and work on the first only, then uncover it.
5.challenge: Ask what happens with “this year” in December, when the year is almost over.
5.monitoring: Whether she states the pattern before the reveal, and whether her own sentences follow it.
5.evidence: Her own two sentences, in her words.
5.transition: Move on when the reveal has been read and she has made one sentence of each kind.

6.goal: To clarify the form, meaning and sound of the two verb forms with numbers, and to place her own sentence from screen 2.
run: Read the table with her, one row at a time.
Read her sentence from screen 2 back to her and ask the question on screen.
If the sentence had a mismatch, ask her to say it again with the verb the period needs.
exact: Reading her sentence back: “You said: ‘…’. Was that period over, or still open?”
On the sound row: “Say it fast: it’s gone up. Can you hear the has?”
6.expected: From the table: past simple for a period that is over (rose, went, hired, was) with in May, last quarter, between January and June; has or have with the past participle for a period that is still open (has risen, has gone up, have stayed) with since July, this year, so far, over the past three months; from… to…, by, at around for the change; has usually weak, as in it’s gone up. For her own sentence, the answer depends on what she said; if she said “Absenteeism didn’t change since January”, the clearer version is “Absenteeism hasn’t changed since January.”
6.support: If the table is too much at once, cover the last two rows until the first three are clear.
6.challenge: Ask her why “yesterday” takes the past simple even though it is very recent, using the box under the table.
6.monitoring: Whether she can tell you, about her own sentence, whether the period was over.
6.evidence: Her sentence from screen 2 and the version she says now.
6.transition: Move on when the table has been read and her sentence has been placed.

7.goal: To produce the two forms with their periods, first in writing and then out loud.
7.interaction: S says each verb form; T types it on screen. Then T–S, spoken.
run: For each of the five sentences, she says the verb in brackets in the form the period needs, and you type it on screen. Then press Check.
Ask her to say the five sentences out loud. Correct the form here: this is the screen where that is the point.

Play the three sentences at the bottom of the screen one at a time. Their words stay hidden: ask her to say which period each one is about and to repeat one with the weak has. Open the words with Show the words only if she needs to read a sentence after two listens.
7.expected: “Turnover rose to 14.6% in the second quarter.” · “Since July, it has gone up again.” · “We hired 40 people in May.” · “So far, 22 of them have stayed.” · “Overtime went from 13 to 30 hours a week between January and June.” Closed periods take the past simple; since July and so far take the present perfect.
7.support: If a form does not come, ask her to find the time words in the sentence first.
7.challenge: Ask her to change one sentence to the other period, for example “In July, it went up again.”
7.monitoring: Whether the forms are right when she says them, and whether has stays weak.
7.evidence: How many of the five she said correctly without help.
7.transition: Move on when the five have been said out loud.

8.goal: To choose the numbers for her update, option A or option B, and to note each change with its period.
8.interaction: T–S to choose, then S alone, writing on paper.
run: Read the two options with her and let her choose.
Give her about four minutes to note three numbers on paper: what each was, what it is now, and the period for each change. Notes, not sentences.
Tell her that on the next screen she gives the update from her notes.
exact: Before she starts: “For each number, write three things: before, now, and when.”
8.expected: Three short notes with a starting figure, a current figure and a period each. For option B: turnover 9.2% to 14.6% in the second quarter and 15.1% since July; overtime 13 to 30 hours between January and June and around 31 since; hires 40 in May, 22 stayed so far. For option A, any three indicators with a period each.
8.support: If she cannot find three numbers from her work, two from her work and one from option B is fine.
8.challenge: Ask her to add, for one number, a change in both kinds of period.
8.monitoring: Whether the period is written next to each number.
8.evidence: The option she chose and whether each note has a period.
8.transition: Move on when the three numbers are noted.

9.goal: To give the update from her notes, choosing the verb each period needs, and to answer a colleague's questions about when.
9.interaction: Role-play. You are a colleague from work, in the US, who asks her questions; she gives the update.
run: Read the task and the list on screen with her.
Let her give the first number. Then ask the first question below, and continue with the others as her update goes on.
The sentence starters stay closed. Open them only if she stops, and close them again. Leave corrections for screen 11; write down one sentence as she says it.
exact: “Since when has it been that high?”
“And has it gone down at all since then?”
9.expected: Three numbers, each with the before, the now and the period, and short answers to your questions with the verb the period needs. For option B: “Turnover rose to 14.6% in the second quarter, and since July it has gone up again, to 15.1%.” To “Since when has it been that high?” — “Since July.” To “When did that start?” — “It started in the second quarter.” To “Has it gone down at all since then?” — “No, it hasn't. It has stayed at around 15%.” For option A the figures are hers; the check is the match between period and verb.
9.support: If she stops, point at the next item on the list before you open the starters.
9.challenge: Ask for one number that went up in one period and down in another.
9.monitoring: Whether the present perfect survives at speed, and whether each number keeps its period.
9.evidence: One sentence of the update, word for word, for the boards on screen 11.
9.transition: Move on when she has given the three numbers and finished with the one that worries her most.

10.goal: To keep the conversation going after the update: answer two more questions from the same colleague, one of them based on something that did not happen, and ask one back.
10.interaction: T–S, unscripted. You are still the same colleague, with two more questions.
run: Ask the two questions below, one at a time.
After each answer, wait. Give her time to add the period.
Then ask her to put one question to you about the figures you need, and answer it.
exact: Question 1: “When did overtime start to fall?”
Question 2: “How many of the people you hired this year have left so far?”
Handing the turn over: “Anything you need from me?”
10.expected: Two answers and one question from her. Question 1 is based on something that did not happen: a complete answer corrects it, for example “It hasn't fallen. It went up to 30 hours between January and June, and it has stayed at around 31 since then.” Question 2, for option B: “We hired 40 people in May, and 18 of them have left so far.” For option A, any figure with so far and the present perfect. Her question can be as small as “Which period do you need the figures for?”.
10.support: If she answers question 1 as if overtime had fallen, point at the dashboard and ask “Did it fall?”
10.challenge: Push once: “But it must have fallen a bit this month.” Let her answer from the figure.
10.monitoring: Whether she corrects the false premise without being prompted, and which form she uses for so far.
10.evidence: What she did with the false premise, and whether she asked a question of her own.
10.transition: Move on when she has answered the two questions and asked one.

11.goal: To compare her sentence from the start of the lesson with the same sentence now, and to run the update again for a listener who only wants the cost.
11.interaction: T–S, filling the boards together, then the replay.
run: Write one thing that worked and one point to improve in the boards on screen.
Write her sentence from screen 2 in the third box, and the same sentence as she would say it now in the fourth.
Open the replay. You are still the same colleague, and this time you only ask about money. She keeps the period with every number.
exact: Opening the replay: “I just need the cost. What has changed since the second quarter?”
11.expected: A shorter update about cost, with periods and matching forms. A complete version for option B: “In the second quarter 48 people left, which was roughly $234,000. Since July the rate has gone up again, so the cost has gone up too.” For option A, her own figures with the same match between period and verb.
11.support: Point at the line on screen and let her use it word for word the first time.
11.challenge: Ask a second cost question with a closed period: “And last year?”
11.monitoring: Whether the point to improve from the boards appears in the replay.
11.evidence: The sentence from screen 2 next to the sentence now. It is the main record of the lesson.
11.transition: Move on when the replay has been said.

12.goal: To close on what was worked on, let her say how confident she feels, and leave the homework said out loud.
12.interaction: T–S, going through the recap and the confidence scale together.
run: Go through the recap list with her and tick what was done.
Let her fill the confidence scale herself.
Read the three lines on the right and say the homework out loud.
exact: The homework, said out loud: “This week, when you talk about a number, say the period first and let it choose the verb.”
12.expected: The recap has six lines, and all six were done if the lesson ran to the end: telling a closed period from an open one, noticing how the time words decide the verb, saying the change with from, to, by and at, using both forms in one update, answering questions about when, and correcting a question based on something that did not happen. The confidence scale is hers, and it may come out lower than what you saw.
12.support: If she marks everything low, read her two sentences from the boards on screen 11.
12.challenge: Ask which number she will describe this way first this week.
12.monitoring: Whether her self-assessment matches what you observed. The gap is worth noting.
12.evidence: Her confidence marks, and anything she said about the pre-class.
12.transition: End here. The next lesson closes the block: she presents what turnover costs in dollars to leaders in the US.
